standard.title: Memorised passwords
standard.description: access their school account using a memorised password and explain why it should be easy to remember, but hard for others to guess
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can access their school account using a recorded username and password (AC9TDI2P06). They know that accounts require credentials. They have not yet memorised credentials independently or reasoned about what makes a password strong (easy to remember, hard to guess).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students access their school account using a memorised password and explain the principles that make a password both memorable and secure.

nodes.label: Why passwords keep accounts private
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why keeping a password private protects their data
nodes.minimum_width: Explain in one or two sentences why a password should be kept secret and what happens if someone else learns it
nodes.typical_width: Explain how passwords protect personal work and data stored in accounts; describe a scenario where someone learns another person's password and explain the consequence
wider: Discuss why shared device passwords (e.g. a school tablet shared between classes) create different security challenges compared to personal account passwords — explore how the school manages this
Investigate what data is stored in a school account and who can access it with the password — connect this to AC9TDI4P09 (personal data in online accounts)
success_criteria: States that a password keeps others from accessing the account
Connects password secrecy to data protection, not just 'the rules'
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not connect password secrecy to data protection (treating it as just a rule) cannot reason about what makes a password strong in N2 — the 'hard to guess' criterion only makes sense if students understand what guessing enables.

nodes.label: What makes a password strong
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what makes a password easy to remember but hard for others to guess, and give an example
nodes.minimum_width: Explain at least one characteristic of a strong password (e.g. uses unrelated but memorable words, is not an obvious personal detail) and give an example
nodes.typical_width: Explain that a strong password balances memorability and security; describe techniques for creating memorable-but-secure passwords (e.g. three unrelated words); distinguish between strong and weak passwords with reasons
wider: Investigate why common password choices (names, birthdays, 'password') are weak — discuss what information about a person could be used to guess a weak password and why this is a risk
Explore how passphrase-style passwords (multiple unrelated words) are both more memorable and more secure than complex single-word passwords — explain the reasoning

response_modes.reason: Students initially assess password strength by complexity (symbols and numbers = strong) rather than by unpredictability. Multiple examples of why personally meaningful information makes passwords guessable — and why random but memorable combinations work — reframe the concept from complexity to unpredictability.

success_criteria: Names at least one feature that makes a password hard to guess
Names at least one feature that makes a password easy to remember
